articles.title: Spain and China are cosying up - to the anger of many in the EU
articles.summary: Amid global tumult, the two countries alliance is not the only unlikely pairing.
articles.preview: On the streets of Barcelona, fiery red and gold Chinese dragons (presumably with very sweaty people inside the costumes) danced among delighted crowds, while Chinese acrobats elicited gasps of amazement as they rolled, tossed and threw spherical lanterns in the air, keeping - as if by magic - the candle inside them upright at all times. Shanghai made history this week: the first Asian metropolis to be invited as the city of honour to Barcelona's famously rambunctious cultural festival, La Merce.
articles.body:
On the streets of Barcelona, fiery red and gold Chinese dragons (presumably with very sweaty people inside the costumes) danced among delighted crowds, while Chinese acrobats elicited gasps of amazement as they rolled, tossed and threw spherical lanterns in the air, keeping - as if by magic - the candle inside them upright at all times.

Shanghai made history this week: the first Asian metropolis to be invited as the city of honour to Barcelona's famously rambunctious cultural festival, La Merce. Vast street processions here are overwhelmingly aimed at celebrating centuries-old Catalan traditions. So it was quite something to witness velvet-clad Catalan pipers, sashaying down Barcelona's main boulevards, their medieval tunes intermingling with lilting music that accompanied flocks of brightly dressed Chinese performers.

Shanghai Vice Mayor Lu Shan flew to Barcelona to speak at La Merce's opening ceremony. Chinese and Catalan cultural traditions differ in form, he remarked, but they share "a common spirit".

Spain and China are experiencing a period of mutual appreciation. But that sense of bonhomie is far from shared across the EU.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has visited China's President Xi Jinping four times in as many years. He's urged the EU as a whole to improve relations with China since Donald Trump's re-election two years ago.

Sanchez's move has sparked resentment and disapproval among a number of Spain's European partners who view Beijing as a strategic rival and possible geopolitical threat to the EU. Privately, they ask if Madrid's welcoming stance - opening up its market to Chinese businesses - is enabling China to become the (economic) enemy within the bloc too.

Pedro Sanchez is not the only EU leader going off piste. Global volatility means other EU countries feel squeezed and exposed and unsure they can rely on America under President Trump. His policy on trade and defence is seen as unpredictable and, at times, aggressive. And so EU member states are selecting strategic partners that they believe suit their national needs, even if that alienates or irritates fellow member states.

So do these new-found alliances risk a permanent splintering of unity in the EU or even Nato?

Spain accused of self-interest

Germany and France - the EU's biggest powers - have just united around a more aggressive approach towards China. They want to give Brussels the muscle to shut subsidised Chinese competitors out of the EU market to address ballooning trade imbalances with Beijing that the European Commission claims have reached a whopping â¬1bn (Â£850m) a day.

Other EU countries fret about China's tight relationship with Russia. Beijing has denied helping Moscow's war effort in Ukraine but defence experts point to technological and economic support from China, which they say has enabled Russia to sustain its military assault.

That's why, as Spain enthusiastically courts Beijing, it stands accused of looking after its own, rather than wider European interests.

"It's a bit chicken and egg. Did Spain distance itself from European allies, or did they distance themselves from us?" asks Victor Cortizo, a lawyer and academic specialising in Sino-Spanish relations.

"I think it's more us. It's Spain. But legitimately so. Realpolitik is a thing. If I get closer to China because that attracts Chinese investment and bolsters my economy, then that is strategically more appealing than supporting allies who are also only looking out for themselves."

Cortizo and I were surrounded by towers of crates as we spoke, at the end of the longest freight rail link in the world. It runs over 13,000km (8,000 miles) between Yiwu in eastern China and Madrid, largely bringing car parts and electrical goods to Spain and transporting delicacies like Spanish ham and red wine back to China. The link is a symbol of the burgeoning relations between the two countries.

"Our prime minister has made the decision to pursue national gain over EU relations," Cortizo told me. "Chinese investment in Spain has doubled over the last year alone."

Rising Chinese investment

According to ICEX Spain Trade and Investment, the Spanish government's trade and investment agency, Chinese investments in Spain are surging, driven in particular by investments in new battery gigafactories and car plants.

Cortizo thinks Spain could become Beijing's preferred European country to invest in now that Hungary is no longer governed by pro-China Viktor Orban, under whom Hungary was dubbed "China's gateway into Europe".

"US investment is sinking and Chinese investment [is] rising in relevance here," Cortizo told me.

The US remains Spain's largest single foreign investor but net investment was down by around â¬1bn, according to Spain's Economy Ministry.

Spanish society now has a far more favourable attitude towards China than towards the US, its traditional ally.

According to a Pew Research Center poll published this summer, 54% of Spaniards said they had a favourable opinion of China compared to 30% who viewed the US favourably.

China makes it easy to trade, Cortizo told me, while the US (through Trump's tariffs and the effects of the war in Iran) has made it far harder. Meanwhile, Spaniards have seen the US president threatening their prime minister with economic sanctions when he doesn't agree to Donald Trump's demands to increase defence spending to 5% of GDP or allow US bases in Spain to be used as part of attacks on Iran.

That's why China is viewed by many in Spain as more reliable than the US.

And when the major Chinese car manufacturer Chery Automobile chose Spain for its first European manufacturing and operations hub two years ago, it breathed life back into then-defunct Spanish brand Ebro.

"Chinese companies are investing in car manufacturing in Spain, filling the gaps we had," says Cortizo.

But critics worry Chinese factories on Spanish soil will weaken the EU single market.

There isn't just Chery in Barcelona. Chinese battery and stationary-energy-storage company Hithium plans to invest in Navarra in the north of Spain and battery manufacturer CATL is involved in building a lithium iron phosphate battery gigafactory in Zaragoza, 200 miles west of Barcelona. Critics fear these projects are part of Chinese companies' efforts to localise production in the EU to evade tariffs on imports of Chinese electric vehicles.

However, Miguel Otero, China specialist at Madrid's ElCano Royal Institute, accuses Spain's European allies of being condescending and hypocritical.

"France, Italy, Germany, they all have their own strategic relationship with China," he tells me. "Spain isn't going much further. It's been catching up with them." In fact, he says, now that Europe can no longer rely fully on the US, Spain's priority is to diversify. It wants to do business not just with China but also Canada, Brazil, India and Africa. Spain is not China-obsessed, he says.

But there's also the question of security.

On his latest trip to Beijing in April, Prime Minister Sanchez met the founder of Chinese wind turbine manufacturer Ming Yang, which had just had its plans to open the UK's largest wind turbine manufacturing plant in the Highlands blocked on national security grounds.

This followed uproar in the EU after Spain's Ministry of the Interior awarded Chinese tech giant Huawei a â¬12.3m contract to store and manage sensitive judicial wiretap data last year.

MEPs from several political groups in the European Parliament said Spain's contract could endanger the EU as a whole.

"When you introduce a high-risk vendor... we do not just risk a localised data breach, we risk poisoning the well of European intelligence sharing," said Markéta Gregorová, a Czech Pirate Party MEP, part of the Greens group back in February.

Juan Ignacio Zoido Ãlvarez, a member of Spain's centre-right opposition party, said the decision puts "the entirety of the EU at risk".

Spain's defence ministry continues to deny there is any risk, but former US Ambassador to Nato Julianne Smith, the co-founder of geostrategic advisory firm Clarion Strategies, warns the episode could really erode European cohesion.

"As EU countries seek ways to hedge against what some see as an unpredictable and unreliable America, they have to be careful not to rush towards alternatives that stand to weaken the EU's collective hand," she tells me.

"Some of those growing relationships, such as Canada's rapidly expanding relationship with the EU, could produce real dividends," she added. "But others, such as Spain's decision to deepen its relationship with China, could further derail the EU's ability to speak with one voice and create added security vulnerabilities for both Spain and wider Europe."

More emerging alliances

Spain is far from alone amongst EU countries in striking up controversial alliances.

Finland has a massive 1,300km-long land border with Russia. This has left it feeling exposed since Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Finland already has the highest rate of civilian firearm ownership per capita in the EU. It has the largest reserve military force in both the EU and Nato. It has built cavities under bridges that can be packed with explosives, should Russian armoured vehicles enter its territory. This is a country that believes military preparedness is an existential necessity.

In 2022, it decided there was safety in numbers. Helsinki ditched its traditional strategic neutrality and rushed to join Nato.

Now though, there are fears that Washington might not respect the alliance's mutual defence clause in case of an attack on a member country.

No longer confident the US would come to the rescue if needed, Finland has turned to Israel to purchase advanced defence equipment, including the David's Sling air-defence system and Spike anti-tank missiles.

Finland renewed its contract with Israel at the height of the recent Gaza war despite its government having publicly expressed considerable reservations about Israeli activity in the occupied Palestinian territories and at a time when many other EU countries also feel deep unease about Israel's policies and activities in Gaza and the West Bank.

"There is a sense in Finland that we can't always afford [to have] a moral superiority. Survival comes at a price," says Minna Alander, a fellow with the Transatlantic Defence and Security Programme at the Center for European Policy Analysis (CEPA).

"Finns and political opposition parties do question whether Israel is a country whose defence industry they want to support [because of its actions in Gaza and the West Bank] but the Finnish government has kept out of the debate, saying the deal with Israel fulfils Finland's needs," she tells me.

In the end, Alander says her fellow Finns have "a less sentimental mentality".

Greece's shift

Greece also feels threatened by a far bigger, immediate neighbour. It perceives Turkey as a "constant and significant danger to its national security and sovereignty", Nick Malkoutzis, co-founder of political analysis website MacroPolis, tells me.

In the past, the US mediated disputes between the two countries. Both are members of Nato. But under Donald Trump, Nato insiders say the US is increasingly perceived as missing in action politically and diplomatically, with Washington's focus very much elsewhere.

In late August, Greece and Israel signed one of the largest defence export deals in both countries' histories. The "Achilles Shield" agreement provides Athens with Israeli technology aimed at protecting Greece against a range of threats, including drones, aircraft and missiles.

There is a history of public sympathy with the Palestinian cause in Greece and many people have been sceptical about ever closer relations with Israel. But Malkoutsis says the public and political reaction to the "mega-deal" with Israel has been "more muted than might have been expected".

He says this is because there is a bottom line - a common understanding of the fundamental need for Greece to strengthen its security in relation to Turkey that takes priority over everything else.

With Israel a close ally of Washington, Greece hopes that "buying Israeli" will also help maintain decent relations with the US, even in these turbulent times.

But it's a delicate dance because Greece and Finland both very much want to be seen as "good Europeans", feeding into the European collective, according to Malkoutsis.

He says EU countries "scrambling in all directions" complicate everyone getting on the same page and speaking with one voice on defence and security which is the opposite of what Brussels and Nato say they want.

That said, European countries banding together in smaller groups to pursue common interests is nothing new. The E3 "gang", composed of the UK, Germany and France, was originally formed in 2003 to co-ordinate diplomatic negotiations with Iran in the hope of a nuclear deal. It's now a more ad hoc communication channel for Europe's three largest military and economic powers.

Nordic and Arctic nations have their own formats for working together to promote regional defence, while the "Visegrad Four" made up of Czechia, Hungary, Poland and Slovakia was for many years a well-known pressure group in EU circles.

However, Nato and the EU are convinced that the continent is under intense pressure, unprecedented since the end of the World War Two. Their leaders say it is time to form a united front. An aggressive Russia growls threateningly at the door, bolstered by Beijing, while the United States, Europe's former best friend abroad, seems, at best, distracted by other priorities.

Splintering, fracturing and rampant "mini-lateralism" will only be applauded by Europe's adversaries, they believe. China and Russia are watching closely.

articles.title: Legge elettorale al via alla Camera: la fiducia del governo e lo sciopero della fame di Magi
articles.summary: AGI - La legge elettorale torna alla Camera in terza lettura, con il governo che si prepara a porre tre fiducie su altrettanti articoli modificati a Palazzo Madama e Riccardo Magi che annuncia uno sciopero della fame contro quello che definisce "un colpo di stato elettorale che vuole consentire a una minoranza nel Paese di diventare maggioranza schiacciante in Parlamento". La legge elettorale e lo sciopero della fame Il leader di +Europa lancia la protesta durante una conferenza stampa, convocata ieri 30 settembre alla Camera. "Da oggi inizierò un digiuno per ottenere la modifica almeno delle parti peggiori di questa norma e consentire di presentare le liste con la firma digitale", dice. "Noi lotteremo fino all'ultimo per modificare questa legge e se non sarà modificata in Parlamento continueremo la battaglia nel paese attraverso i ricorsi in tribunale", assicura Magi. Che prepara, in parallelo, una serie di "iniziative non violente e ricorsi in sedi giurisdizionali" su cui +Europa "sta già lavorando". I nodi della protesta Al centro dei rilievi, condivisi dalle altre opposizioni, l'equa rappresentanza dei generi, perché "si travolge completamente l'equilibrio di genere nelle candidature" e la norma che introduce un tetto di firme più alto per chi si presenta alle elezioni per la prima volta. "Sono state aumentate a dismisura le firme necessarie per presentarsi alle elezioni. Di fatto sono necessarie 450.000 firme per una nuova forza politica che vuole cimentarsi con la democrazia elettorale. Una cosa incredibile e sicuramente incostituzionale", osserva il segretario di +Europa. La fase finale del percorso parlamentare del testo In parallelo alla protesta di stampo Radicale di Magi, entra nell'ultima fase il percorso parlamentare del testo, dopo che - a luglio scorso - la maggioranza era 'andata sotto', con il voto segreto, sull'emendamento che introduceva le preferenze, poi passate al Senato. La legge elettorale, ieri pomeriggio, è tornata in Aula alla Camera, dopo l'approvazione del testo e l'ok al mandato al relatore in commission e Affari Costituzionali . Oltre a quelli di maggioranza, ci saranno anche quattro relatori di minoranza: Federico Fornaro (Pd), Filiberto Zaratti (Avs), Carmela Auriemma (M5s), oltre a Magi. Oggi, a partire dalle 12, è previsto un unico voto sulle cinque pregiudiziali di costituzionalità chieste dalle opposizioni. A quanto si apprende, gli emendamenti presentati dalle opposizioni sono circa sessanta, gli stessi depositati in commissione agli articoli del testo modificati in Senato, anche se - con l'apposizione della fiducia - le proposte di modifica decadranno. Comunque, quello di oggi è un primo 'test' d'Aula per la tenuta della maggioranza, dato che probabilmente le minoranze chiederanno lo scrutinio segreto, come era stato a luglio sull'emendamento sulle preferenze, che poi è stato bocciato grazie a i 'franchi tiratori' tra le fila del centrodestra. Sul punto un esponente di centrodestra che segue il dossier dice di "non avere dubbi" sulla compattezza della maggioranza, anche in vista dei voti successivi nell'Aula di Montecitorio. E FdI serra i ranghi. "Mi sembra che Giorgia Meloni sia stata chiara. Se il provvedimento non passa si va a casa. La fiducia è stata messa per questo motivo", dice il capogruppo dei meloniani alla Camera, Galeazzo Bignami. In caso di bocciatura delle pregiudiziali dovrebbe riunirsi già oggi una Conferenza dei capigruppo, per fissare il timing dei lavori. Su tre dei quattro articoli modificati a Palazzo Madama, il governo dovrebbe porre la fiducia , che dovrebbe essere votata venerdì, con il voto palese. Mentre, un'altra 'prova' con lo scrutinio segreto è probabile con il voto finale sul provvedimento, che dovrebbe tenersi la prossima settimana, tra mercoledì e giovedì.

articles.title: Ethiopia and Eritrea cut diplomatic ties as northern conflict escalates
articles.summary: The diplomatic fallout comes as Ethiopian forces battle rebel fighters across its northern region.
articles.preview: Ethiopia and Eritrea have severed diplomatic relations as renewed fighting in northern Ethiopia raises fears of a wider regional conflict. On Thursday, Ethiopia announced that it was closing its embassy in the Eritrean capital, Asmara, and ordered 10 Eritrean diplomats to leave the country within 48 hours, accusing them of activities that threatened national security. Eritrea responded by cutting diplomatic relations, saying Ethiopia's decision had left it with no choice but to take reciprocal action.
articles.body:
Ethiopia and Eritrea have severed diplomatic relations as renewed fighting in northern Ethiopia raises fears of a wider regional conflict.

On Thursday, Ethiopia announced that it was closing its embassy in the Eritrean capital, Asmara, and ordered 10 Eritrean diplomats to leave the country within 48 hours, accusing them of activities that threatened national security.

Eritrea responded by cutting diplomatic relations, saying Ethiopia's decision had left it with no choice but to take reciprocal action.

The diplomatic confrontation came hours after powerful explosions were heard overnight in Ethiopian capital, Addis Ababa, including near Ethiopia's military headquarters.

It follows a sharp deterioration in relations between the neighbours, with Addis Ababa accusing Eritrea of supporting an alliance of armed groups fighting the Ethiopian government â an allegation Asmara has repeatedly denied.

Ethiopia said it was expelling 10 Eritrean diplomats who "pose a direct threat to Ethiopia's national security" and would shut its embassy in Asmara.

In response, Eritrea announced late on Thursday that it was severing diplomatic ties with Ethiopia, describing Addis Ababa's decision as "astounding".

"Eritrea has no option but to reciprocate in kind and sever all diplomatic ties with Ethiopia," its foreign ministry said, warning of "negative corollaries" from the decision.

The diplomatic fallout comes as Ethiopian federal forces battle fighters from the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) and its allies across parts of Tigray, Afar and Amhara.

- Are Ethiopians marching back to war in Tigray?

- Published6 days ago

- Why are Ethiopia's rebels joining forces?

- Published3 days ago

The latest hostilities are the most serious since a peace agreement ended the devastating Tigray war in 2022. An African Union mediator previously estimated that about 600,000 people had died during that two-year conflict.

Last month, the TPLF joined six other armed movements, including the Fano militia from Amhara, to form an alliance whose stated objective is to remove Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government from power.

Ethiopia has accused Eritrea of helping the alliance.

A pro-government militia commander fighting in Tigray also told the BBC that Eritrean soldiers had been involved on the front lines. The BBC has not independently verified the allegation.

But in a rare interview with the BBC before diplomatic relations were severed, Eritrea's Information Minister Yemane Gebremeskel rejected the accusations.

He told BBC Tigrinya that Ethiopia's governing Prosperity Party was blaming neighbouring countries to divert attention from conflicts and other problems within Ethiopia.

The two countries were allies during the 2020-2022 Tigray war, when Eritrean troops fought alongside Ethiopian federal forces against the TPLF.

But relations have deteriorated significantly since then, particularly over Ethiopia's push for direct access to the Red Sea. Asmara accuses Ethiopia of pursuing what it describes as an increasingly hostile policy over the Red Sea.

Landlocked Ethiopia lost its coastline when Eritrea became independent in 1993.

Abiy has repeatedly argued that access to the sea is essential to Ethiopia's long-term economic and security interests, while Eritrea has accused his government of harbouring ambitions over its ports.

The latest diplomatic confrontation came hours after loud explosions were heard on Wednesday night in Addis Ababa, close to the headquarters of the intelligence service.

A source linked to the opposition alliance told Reuters news agency that its forces had carried out drone attacks in the capital. Ethiopian authorities have not confirmed what caused the explosions, and there have been no official reports of casualties or significant damage.

Residents in two areas of Addis Ababa separately told the BBC that they heard powerful explosions during the night. One resident near the intelligence headquarters said the blast was loud enough to trigger car alarms.

The explosions came hours after Ethiopia's National Intelligence and Security Service imposed an indefinite ban on drone flights over Addis Ababa and surrounding areas, citing the need to protect senior officials, important infrastructure and public events.

Meanwhile, fighting continues across northern Ethiopia.

Federal forces and their allies appear to have made gains in southern Tigray and are advancing towards Mekelle, the regional capital. In Alamata, a doctor told the BBC earlier this week that at least 52 civilians had been killed during three days of intense fighting.

The TPLF has also been fighting in neighbouring Afar, which lies along Ethiopia's crucial transport corridor to Djibouti and the sea. Tens of thousands of people are estimated to have fled their homes there.

Both the Ethiopian government and the TPLF accuse the other of starting the latest hostilities. Tigrayan authorities say their forces were responding to a federal offensive and drone strikes, while Addis Ababa says Tigrayan fighters launched attacks after taking control of federally administered airports in Tigray.

Independent verification remains difficult because journalists have limited access to the conflict areas and communications across much of Tigray have been disrupted.

The African Union has urged Ethiopia, Eritrea and Egypt to exercise restraint and resolve their differences through diplomatic channels, warning against actions that could further destabilise the region.

The UN has also warned that the deteriorating security situation is severely disrupting humanitarian work in northern Ethiopia. UN spokesman Stéphane Dujarric said drone activity and air strikes were putting civilians, vital infrastructure and aid operations at risk, while insecurity and road closures were restricting humanitarian movements.

The UN has called on all sides to guarantee safe and unhindered access to people in need.

articles.title: FAO official says he lost his job for criticising Israeli policies in Gaza
articles.summary: The FAO official said he was told his contract would not be renewed over an alleged breach of impartiality on Gaza.
articles.preview: FAO director said he was informed his contract would not be renewed because of allegedly breaching impartiality rules. A senior UN agency director has said that he lost his job because he criticised Israeli policies in Gaza. Ben Davis, who had been Director of Rural Transformation and Gender Equality at the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), told AFP news agency on Wednesday that he was informed in July that his contract would not be renewed because he had allegedly breached impartiality rules.
articles.body:
FAO director said he was informed his contract would not be renewed because of allegedly breaching impartiality rules.

A senior UN agency director has said that he lost his job because he criticised Israeli policies in Gaza.

Ben Davis, who had been Director of Rural Transformation and Gender Equality at the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), told AFP news agency on Wednesday that he was informed in July that his contract would not be renewed because he had allegedly breached impartiality rules.

He said that he was accused of organising weekly silent protests at the Rome-based organisation.

“They accused me of organising these moments of silence on the situation of starvation and famine in Gaza,” Davis said.

Davis was also criticised for a report he worked on about food availability in Gaza and humanitarian law, published in May.

“We were told to take it down,” he said. “We weren’t allowed to make any references to humanitarian law.”

‘Game of human rights’

FAO Director-General Qu Dongyu appeared to warn FAO staff on Tuesday that “we don’t allow you to play the game here of human rights”.

He was speaking in public comments made at the start of a filmed session on forestry.

“Of course, human rights is very important, but we have the human rights agency in Geneva,” he added. “If you want to take care, go there.

“That’s why some senior members play the political game here, I fire him … You should follow the FAO constitution … You are against staff regulations … But I’m a very soft person, I didn’t fire that many,” he said.

“I will fire more people if they are against the law,” he added.

FAO did not respond to an AFP request for comment.

Asked if he thought the director-general’s comments were about him, Davis said “absolutely”.

“He has already scolded me in public in the past for being too political.”

Davis also said he was “concerned” about the director-general’s comments on firing more people.

Hundreds of people attended the moments of silence at their height, while now there are only 30 to 40 people coming on a weekly basis, he said.

Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza has killed over 74,000 people since October 2023, and at least 1,431 Palestinians have been killed in Israeli attacks since the so-called ceasefire between Hamas and Israel was agreed upon in October 2025.

articles.body:
Massive US military deployment in the Middle East includes 50,000 troops, F-35s and Marines to pressure Tehran.

The United States is deploying a third US aircraft carrier to the waters around Iran, a US official told Al Jazeera, as the war enters its eighth month and both sides weigh escalation and diplomatic engagement.

The official told Al Jazeera that the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group left its San Diego base on Sunday, bound for the region, followed a day later by the Makin Island Marine Expeditionary Force, carrying more than 2,000 Marines.

Recommended Stories

list of 3 items

- list 1 of 3Iranians stock up on food and medicine as fears of new US fighting grow

- list 2 of 3US-Iran talks in New York: What’s the latest?

- list 3 of 3Trump administration ‘must be changed’: Iran’s IRGC appeals to US voters

By the end of November, the official said, three aircraft carriers and two amphibious landing groups will be positioned around Iran.

The official said the concentration of force would hand President Donald Trump a wider menu of options if he decides to act.

Al Jazeera’s Tanya Noury, reporting from Washington, said the new deployment includes thousands of troops and extra air power, including F-35 fighter jets, layered on top of the roughly 50,000 US service members already stationed in the region.

The goal, Noury said, citing sources inside the Pentagon and White House, is to keep military options “on the table” for Trump regardless of how diplomacy unfolds, with the Pentagon not planning to withdraw any assets even if an agreement with Iran is reached. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has said forces are “ready to go” should Trump order new strikes.

Trump himself has kept the threat alive in public. He told Fox News he believes the US is “going to win the war” with Iran “very soon”, while suggesting in other remarks that a return to military action “is possible” but something he would rather not spell out before November’s midterm elections.

Washington has paired the show of force with new economic pressure, sanctioning Iran’s rail and automotive conglomerates this week, as the Treasury Department called the new measures an effort to drain what remains of Tehran’s revenue.

Diplomatic track

Parallel to the military build-up, Iran has pushed a seven-day roadmap, conveyed through Qatar, that would see it reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume nuclear talks in exchange for an end to the US naval blockade, sanctions relief and a regional ceasefire covering Lebanon and Yemen.

The plan was then rejected by Trump.

US Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz told NBC the plan’s demand for frozen funds and sanctions relief was non-negotiable, noting “these aren’t just the United States’ sanctions … these are global sanctions”, and pointing to seven UN Security Council resolutions against an Iranian nuclear weapons programme.

Iran’s response, in the meantime, has been similarly two-pronged.

Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told NBC that Tehran was “fully prepared” to resume the war, before writing on X that “we did not come to New York to sell a war. We came to forge peace.”

Analysts say the mixed signals are deliberate.

Abas Aslani of the Center for Middle East Strategic Studies said the dispute has shifted from whether to negotiate to “who is going to abandon the primary leverage first”, while former US ambassador Richard Schmierer said Trump is caught between delaying past the midterms and the political cost of offering concessions that mirror a June deal he was already criticised for.

Nearly 70 percent of Americans now say the war has not been worth fighting, according to a new AP-NORC poll, with Trump brushing off the slide in his approval ratings by insisting “the pollsters are corrupt”.

articles.title: Seoul warns 'further action' if Ukraine does not apologise over prisoner-of-war row
articles.summary: President Lee Jae Myung also accused Kyiv of "attempting to provoke a war on the Korean Peninsula".
articles.preview: South Korea's President Lee Jae Myung has threatened to take unspecified "further action" if Ukraine does not issue a public apology for revealing that two North Korean prisoners of war had been sent to the South. Ukraine's leader Volodymyr Zelensky made the disclosure to the UN general assembly last week, angering Seoul, who said the move was meant to stay secret. Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha on Thursday described the situation as a "diplomatic misunderstanding", adding that Kyiv was "working" to resolve it.
articles.body:
South Korea's President Lee Jae Myung has threatened to take unspecified "further action" if Ukraine does not issue a public apology for revealing that two North Korean prisoners of war had been sent to the South.

Ukraine's leader Volodymyr Zelensky made the disclosure to the UN general assembly last week, angering Seoul, who said the move was meant to stay secret.

Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha on Thursday described the situation as a "diplomatic misunderstanding", adding that Kyiv was "working" to resolve it.

Lee rejected this characterisation on X, saying it concerned "the dignity of the Korean people and the nation".

Lee's office said last week that it was Ukraine that requested for the move to be kept secret, partly to protect the North Koreans' families, and also because Kyiv wanted to avoid criticism that it had given up an opportunity to exchange the soldiers for Ukrainian prisoners of war.

Zelensky's office responded, saying the two countries had no such agreement to keep the move confidential, further escalating the situation.

Lee himself faced heavy criticism at home after Zelensky's disclosure, with the South Korean opposition accusing him of covering up the transfer to appease Pyongyang.

The two soldiers, who were among thousands of North Koreans supporting Russia in the Ukraine war, had earlier told local media they wanted to be sent to South Korea.

Speaking to Ukrainian media on Thursday, Sybiha, the foreign minister, said he "hopes that this situation will be resolved in the very near future".

"We are working on it. For us, South Korea is an important country. And I really hope for momentum, continuation, and concrete results that we are truly achieving with them," he said.

Lee, in response, accused Kyiv of attempting to "bring war on the Korean Peninsula".

"We express serious regret that, instead of acknowledging the facts of the agreement and apologising, they are talking about an imminent military clash between the North and South," he said in an X post.

Seoul has been sympathetic to Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion, but has adhered to its longstanding policy of not providing lethal weapons to any country engaged in active war.

articles.title: Trump launches midterms campaign blitz amid record low approval ratings
articles.summary: In a series of campaign-style rallies, Trump seeks to boost Republican odds amid Iran war and rising fuel costs.
articles.preview: In a series of campaign-style rallies, Trump seeks to boost Republican odds despite opposition to the Iran war and rising fuel costs. United States President Donald Trump has kicked off a 32-day campaign tour ahead of the November midterm elections that could see his Republican Party hurt by his handling of the war on Iran and the economy. On Thursday, Trump travelled from Washington, DC, for back-to-back rallies in Texas and Oklahoma.
articles.body:
In a series of campaign-style rallies, Trump seeks to boost Republican odds despite opposition to the Iran war and rising fuel costs.

United States President Donald Trump has kicked off a 32-day campaign tour ahead of the November midterm elections that could see his Republican Party hurt by his handling of the war on Iran and the economy.

On Thursday, Trump travelled from Washington, DC, for back-to-back rallies in Texas and Oklahoma.

Recommended Stories

list of 3 items

- list 1 of 3Most Americans say US-Israel war on Iran not worth fighting: Poll

- list 2 of 3US FCC head says controversial Trump ads do not raise concerns

- list 3 of 3Despite praise and White House visits, Trump avoids endorsing Netanyahu

At his first stop in Denton, Texas, Trump sought to shift the narrative around his drooping approval ratings, offering a personal assessment of his administration’s performance.

“I give us an A+ on the government, on economics, on everything,” Trump told a crowd of supporters at the Peterbilt Motors Company, a truck manufacturer.

The president also blamed unfair media coverage for his growing unpopularity, arguing that his pre-election rally blitz was necessary to set the record straight.

“We’re doing an extremely poor job of promotion and an extremely great job of running the country,” Trump said.

But Trump’s poll numbers have raised concerns about Republican prospects ahead of the November 3 midterm election.

Trump himself is not on the ballot, but Republican candidates across the country are seeking to defend the right-wing party’s majorities in both chambers of Congress, as well as key state and local offices.

The economy and Trump’s war on Iran are expected to weigh heavily on the election outcome.

On Thursday, The Associated Press and the NORC Center for Public Affairs Research released new poll results showing that 71 percent of Americans disapprove of the war, which has driven up the price of fuel.

About half of survey respondents also said they were worried they would not be able to afford food and petrol. Only 26 percent approved of Trump’s handling of the economy.

Taking centre stage

Still, despite record low approval ratings, Trump has positioned himself as key to the Republican midterm strategy.

At a first-of-its-kind Republican midterm convention in September, Trump encouraged voters to consider his record while at the ballot box. “I’m asking you to pretend that I’m on the ballot,” he said.

During Thursday’s tour, he touted the impact of his tariff campaign, which he credited with creating thousands of manufacturing jobs.

“For decades, you were heartlessly betrayed by politicians, lousy politicians, who let foreign trade cheaters plunder your wages, loot your factories, close up your jobs,” Trump told Peterbilt workers. “They’d still be doing it if I wasn’t here, believe me.”

Trump’s tariffs, however, have been highly controversial, prompting a series of court challenges. Critics have argued that the sweeping import taxes surpass the president’s constitutional powers.

Trump also used his stump speech to ease concerns about the US-Israel war on Iran, which began on February 28. Both sides have declared victory, though a ceasefire remains elusive.

“Just as I promised, I’m ensuring that Iran will be very quickly ended. I will tell you the energy prices are going to be rapidly, rapidly coming down,” Trump said.

“We’ll win very easily right now,” he added. “I believe right after the election we’ll win, but maybe before the election.”

The war, however, resulted in Iran stopping commercial traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for the global fuel trade.

The price of diesel — the fuel the trucks built at the plant use — soared to record highs of more than $6 per gallon (3.8 litres) last week. Petrol prices have similarly skyrocketed.

Hurting or helping his fellow Republicans?

Trump, however, has acknowledged that the stakes are high for his presidency in the upcoming midterms.

All 435 seats in the House of Representatives are up for grabs, as are 35 seats in the 100-member Senate.

Losing Republican control of either chamber could create roadblocks for Trump’s legislative agenda during the final two years of his second term.

But Trump has also expressed concern that he could be impeached for a third time, after two prior impeachments during his first presidency.

At Thursday’s second stop, in Durant, Oklahoma, the Republican leader repeated that fear. “Pretend I’m running, please,” he told the crowd. “If we don’t win, they’ll end up impeaching me.”

Many of the places Trump is scheduled to visit this month are perceived as reliably Republican voting districts. Following his stops in Texas and Oklahoma on Thursday, Trump will be heading to Alabama, Ohio and Nebraska in the coming days.

Still, some elections that ordinarily would be considered shoo-ins for Republicans have grown more competitive in recent months.

In Texas, for instance, no Democrat has won a statewide race since the 1990s. But this year, Republican Ken Paxton, the state’s attorney general, is struggling to win a Senate contest against Democrat James Talarico.

During both of Thursday’s stops, Trump sought to bolster Paxton’s prospects. At the Peterbilt factory, for instance, he called Paxton “the greatest attorney general in the United States of America”.

“We gotta get this guy elected,” Trump said, before pivoting to criticisms of Talarico, whom Republicans have sought to paint as out of touch with Texas’s large beef industry.

“He’s a vegan,” Trump said of Talarico, repeating an unsubstantiated rumour. “And vegans don’t do well in Texas.”

But leaked audio appeared to show Paxton lamenting the negative impact Trump had by holding the Republican midterm convention in Texas last month.

“It dropped our numbers. Everybody’s numbers dropped,” Paxton reportedly said.

Trump touts social conservatism

Trump has nevertheless used his pre-election tour to highlight social issues he feels will help rally voters to the Republican cause.

On Thursday, he returned to familiar subjects like immigration and transgender rights, which he depicted as a part of the Democrats’ “radical” agenda.

“They want women in men’s sports. They want open borders. They want transgender mutilation for your children,” Trump said. “What the hell are you thinking about, you liberals?”

The president also used his Texas appearance to push back against critics of data centres, despite bipartisan concern.

Critics worry that the rapid growth of artificial intelligence (AI) has fuelled the proliferation of data centres, which require large amounts of electricity and water to process mass data quantities.

While Trump has dismissed fears about AI as largely unfounded, a poll last month found 53 percent of Americans are “extremely” or “very” concerned about the technology’s environmental impacts.

Even fellow Republicans in Texas are responding to public pressure about the growing number of data centres, more than 300 of which are operational, with hundreds more in progress.

In August, Governor Greg Abbott called for an audit of all data centres to map their water and electricity usage, and the following month, Paxton in his role as state attorney general launched an investigation into whether they were complying with water reporting requirements.

Trump nevertheless used his Texas rally to tout the expansion of such enterprises.

“It’s a huge thing. It’s bigger than the industrial revolution,” he said, dismissing the concerns as part of a “scam”. He then explained he had urged AI companies to “take care of the people”.

“They’re making a fortune for the communities,” he added.

articles.title: Netanyahu says Flydubai attacker had 'Islamist radical indoctrination'
articles.summary: Israel's prime minister says the pilot who tried to take over the Flydubai plane clearly intended to "down the plane".
articles.preview: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu says investigations suggest the man who stabbed his fellow pilot and tried to take over a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv had undergone "Islamist radical indoctrination". The Flydubai plane plunged more than 17,000ft (5,200m) two hours into its journey on Wednesday, before passengers and crew overpowered the attacker and retook control to land safely. Netanyahu told Fox News that it was looking "very likely" that the attacker, who he said was an Omani national, "was going to down the plane".
articles.body:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu says investigations suggest the man who stabbed his fellow pilot and tried to take over a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv had undergone "Islamist radical indoctrination".

The Flydubai plane plunged more than 17,000ft (5,200m) two hours into its journey on Wednesday, before passengers and crew overpowered the attacker and retook control to land safely.

Netanyahu told Fox News that it was looking "very likely" that the attacker, who he said was an Omani national, "was going to down the plane".

Meanwhile, the United Arab Emirates (UAE) state news agency reports investigations have begun there to determine "whether the incident was linked to any terrorist activity or purpose".

The Interior Ministry of Saudi Arabia - where the plane made an emergency landing - said that both the pilot and co-pilot had been sent back to the UAE on Thursday morning after medical teams had cleared them.

UAE officials earlier claimed jurisdiction over the incident because the aircraft on which the attack took place is registered there and flies under its flag.

Netanyahu told Fox that once the attacker had been subdued and tied up by passengers and crew, he was "calling out to the aircrew 'kill me, kill me', so it's clear he was suicidal - that's not a question".

"And with all the passengers in there, and if you couple that with what I just told you about the Islamist tendencies, that radicalisation that were found in his background, I think... that'll give us a pretty good clue."

However, he stressed that he did not want to draw any firm conclusions as to motive yet.

Both US President Donald Trump and UAE officials have indicated to the media that Iran may be responsible for the incident, without definitively blaming Tehran.

Trump told reporters on Thursday that Iran would be "hit very hard" if it was deemed to have been involved in the attack.

Pilots from countries without diplomatic relations with Israel were usually not allowed to fly there, Netanyahu said when asked about how the suspected Omani pilot came to be on the plane.

He added: "Obviously there was a loophole here and we're taking care of that among other things... with the full co-operation, I have to say, of the Emirati government, so we're both interested in making sure this doesn't happen again."

Oman has not formally established official ties with Israel, unlike the UAE.

The prime minister was also asked earlier on the same network whether there was an indication if Iran was involved, he replied: "It's too early to say".

- Flydubai passenger describes hugging his children as plane nosedived during attack

- Published16 hours ago

- Who is the 'hero' Indian pilot who was stabbed on Israel-bound flight?

- Published15 hours ago

Both Netanyahu and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi said the stabbed pilot, Indian national Capt Smit Machchhar was a "hero".

India's ambassador to the UAE Deepak Mittal visited Captain Machhar in hospital on Thursday, the Indian Mission confirmed on social media, stating he was "in good health and recovering well".

Preliminary findings from a separate Israeli investigation into the incident, suggest that the alleged attacker intended to crash the plane, an Israeli security source told BBC Arabic.

The source said the investigation - led by Israel's intelligence agency Mossad - interviewed passengers after they arrived in Tel Aviv to establish what had happened on the plane.

Flydubai's flight FZ1073, with more than 170 people on board, took off from Dubai International Airport in the UAE at 03:05 GMT (07:05 local time), en route to Ben Gurion Airport.

Two hours later, the 17,000ft drop in altitude was reported on the plane tracking website Flightradar24 and minutes later the plane signalled an emergency code.

At about 05:40, the plane - which had briefly entered Jordanian airspace - looped back into Saudi Arabia, where it later started its manual descent, landing safely at Tabuk Airport in the north west of Saudi.

Flydubai has since suspended flights between Dubai and Tel Aviv as it carried out its own investigation into the incident.

Israel's Transportation Ministry said the suspension aligns with Netanyahu's directive.

Israeli airlines including El Al, Israir and Arkia said plans were in place to operate rescue flights from Dubai starting on Friday to bring back stranded passengers.

The Transportation Ministry also said it sent an urgent request to Etihad Airlines to increase the number of flights between Abu Dhabi and Tel Aviv.

articles.title: Lula e Bolsonaro Jr divisi anche dalla fede, è guerra di religione
articles.summary: Il cattolico Brasile potrebbe eleggere il primo presidente evangelico. Lite sulla patrona
articles.preview: L'ultimo tratto della campagna elettorale per la presidenza del Brasile è stato segnato da una sorta di guerra religiosa: del resto domenica il Paese più cattolico del mondo potrebbe per la prima volta eleggere un presidente evangelico, neo-pentecostale. Perché a dividere Lula da Bolsonaro Jr non è solo la politica, l'ideologia, il rapporto con Trump, ma anche la fede.
articles.body:
L'ultimo tratto della campagna elettorale per la presidenza del Brasile è stato segnato da una sorta di guerra religiosa: del resto domenica il Paese più cattolico del mondo potrebbe per la prima volta eleggere un presidente evangelico, neo-pentecostale. Perché a dividere Lula da Bolsonaro Jr non è solo la politica, l'ideologia, il rapporto con Trump, ma anche la fede.

Un dato molto sentito in un Paese con circa 100 milioni di battezzati cattolici, circa la metà della popolazione, ma dove soprattutto negli ultimi anni s'è registrata una enorme crescita delle chiese evangeliche che oggi rappresentano circa il 26,9% della popolazione. Non è un caso che Lula sia in testa tra i cattolici con il 48% contro il 29%, secondo l'ultimo sondaggio Quaest, mentre Flavio prevale tra gli evangelici con il 46% contro il 27%.

La miccia che ha fatto scoppiare la polemica tra i due gruppi di fedeli è stata la vicenda su Nostra Signora di Aparecida. Prima Globo Tv, poi diversi esponenti del partito di Lula hanno diffuso la notizia che gli evangelici vicini a Flávio Bolsonaro, in caso di sua vittoria, avrebbero declassato la Vergine da patrona del Brasile a semplice protettrice dei cattolici brasiliani. Flavio ha subito reagito violentemente, parlando di fake news e annunciando ricorsi contro i propalatori di questa indiscrezione. Quindi ha addirittura paragonato questa controversia all'accoltellamento subito dal padre nel 2018, arrivando ad accusare la Conferenza dei vescovi brasiliana (Cnbb) di essere dietro questa manovra contro di lui.

Attacco a cui la Chiesa ha replicato piccata: "La menzogna non può essere combattuta con un'altra menzogna: la Conferenza episcopale non ha prodotto, autorizzato né partecipato alla preparazione o diffusione di informazioni false relative all'attuale processo elettorale. Attribuire alla Cnbb la partecipazione alle strutture di produzione o diffusione di disinformazione, senza fatti e prove, influisce ingiustamente sull'istituzione e non contribuisce alla serenità del processo elettorale".

Detto questo Lula è stato chiaro al riguardo, prendendo molto sul serio la questione: "Sino a quando sarò presidente nessuno potrà toccare la vergine Maria". Ma al di là delle polemiche verbali, nelle ultime ore si sono registrati atti di vandalismo contro immagini sacre della Nostra Signora di Aparecida in diverse regioni del Brasile, nonché attacchi a luoghi di culto dell'Umbanda, una religione afro-brasiliana, in un clima di crescente intolleranza religiosa. E l'area più progressista della Chiesa brasiliana è sempre più convintache, al di là delle smentite ufficiali, gli evangelici minaccino sul serio la patrona. "Altro che fake news, questa di declassare la Vergine è una storia che viene da lontano", spiega all'ANSA Júlio Lancellotti, sacerdote pronipote di italiani calabresi noto per il suo lavoro a favore dei senza tetto di San Paolo.

Il sacerdote fa riferimento a un disegno di legge presentato nel 2007 dall'ex deputato Victório Galli per rimuovere il titolo di "patrona del Brasile" a Nostra Signora di Aparecida, trasformandola in "patrona dei brasiliani cattolici romani".

L'iniziativa è stata accantonata dalla Camera nel 2008. Tuttavia Galli è stato consigliere speciale della Presidenza nel governo di Jair Bolsonaro ed è ora nuovamente candidato a deputato.

"Quindi il progetto può essere rilanciato in qualsiasi momento," ha aggiunto Padre Júlio, che è già stato bersaglio di persecuzioni da parte dei bolsonaristi per la sua difesa della popolazione senza fissa dimora.

Oggi la Vergine è conservata nel Santuario Nazionale di Aparecida, la seconda basilica cattolica più grande e il più grande tempio mariano al mondo, e la data in suo onore, il 12 ottobre, è festa nazionale nel Paese. "Nostra Signora di Aparecida fa parte della cultura brasiliana, è un fenomeno di religiosità popolare che trascende la Chiesa", ha spiegato padre Júlio. Ad ogni modo, la designazione di "patrono del Brasile", come capita con ogni stato al mondo è un titolo "pontificio", e non dello Stato, che al massimo potrebbe solo sopprimere la festività del 12 ottobre. Tuttavia un gesto in tal senso avrebbe un enorme valore simbolico.

articles.title: Trump affida a Musk la pianificazione della guerra del futuro
articles.summary: Elon torna a lavorare col governo. Dalla luna ai robot, l'incarico del Pentagono
articles.preview: Nome in codice 'Project Meridian', ovvero lo studio della guerra del futuro. Pete Hegseth svela la nuova iniziativa del Pentagono e ne affida la guida a Elon Musk, Palmer Luckey e Newt Gingrich, puntando ad anticipare i futuri scenari operativi e a sviluppare tutti gli strumenti necessari per garantire la supremazia militare Usa. Il patron di SpaceX e Tesla, nonché l'uomo più ricco del pianeta, torna dunque a lavorare con l'amministrazione di Donald Trump dopo l'esperienza del 2025 al vertice dell' ambizioso Dipartimento per l'efficienza governativa…
articles.body:
Nome in codice 'Project Meridian', ovvero lo studio della guerra del futuro. Pete Hegseth svela la nuova iniziativa del Pentagono e ne affida la guida a Elon Musk, Palmer Luckey e Newt Gingrich, puntando ad anticipare i futuri scenari operativi e a sviluppare tutti gli strumenti necessari per garantire la supremazia militare Usa. Il patron di SpaceX e Tesla, nonché l'uomo più ricco del pianeta, torna dunque a lavorare con l'amministrazione di Donald Trump dopo l'esperienza del 2025 al vertice dell' ambizioso Dipartimento per l'efficienza governativa (Doge), chiusasi con una clamorosa rottura, lentamente ricucita. Musk sarà affiancato da Luckey, a capo dell'azienda di tecnologie per la difesa Anduril, e da Newt Gingrich, l'ex speaker repubblicano della Camera, e dovrà, avvalendosi del contributo di esperti di hi-tech e di sicurezza nazionale, proporre già le prime soluzioni entro 120 giorni. Project Meridian intende esaminare come l'esercito americano possa utilizzare le nuove tecnologie e condurre la guerra in terreni inesplorati, comprese la Luna, ha spiegato il Dipartimento della Difesa. "Stiamo assistendo a rapidi progressi nell'intelligenza artificiale, nell'autonomia, nell'energia diretta, nella robotica, nelle biotecnologie, tra le altre aree critiche dell'alta tecnologia", ha notato Hegseth.

La guerra della Russia contro l'Ucraina, prima, e quella di Usa e Israele contro l'Iran, poi, hanno fatto emergere in modo chiaro che il modo della potenza militare, intesa come il tradizionale possesso di hardware (missili, carri armati, navi e caccia), non basta più se un drone da poche migliaia di dollari può creare danni ben più gravi. Insieme, "questi nuovi domini, modi di combattere e sviluppi tecnologici modificheranno profondamente la natura della guerra", ha aggiunto il capo del Pentagono, annunciando il progetto.

"Per mantenere il dominio globale, gli Stati Uniti devono anticipare i futuri ambienti operativi", con una postura "volutamente orientata al futuro. Dobbiamo avere l'umiltà di riconoscere che i migliori analisti dei conflitti futuri non si trovano esclusivamente all'interno del Pentagono: esistono evidenti pregiudizi e rischi nel pretendere di porci le domande e, al contempo, di darci le risposte", ha osservato ancora.

Hegseth ha detto che Musk, Luckey e Gingrich, sotto la guida di Emil Michael, sottosegretario alla Difesa per la ricerca e l'ingegneria, "si concentreranno sulla individuazione, sviluppo e impiego operativo di armi e sistemi di cui i nostri figli e nipoti avranno bisogno nel corso della loro vita: il tutto senza limitazioni creative o vincoli, per qualsiasi futuro campo di battaglia, dal sottosuolo terrestre fino a oltre la Luna": perché le forze armate americane "non devono dare per scontati gli attuali vantaggi". Per questo, anche lo Stato maggiore congiunto (Joint Staff) e tutte le forze armate dovranno essere pronti a collegare le proprie iniziative di ricerca e i progetti relativi alla guerra del futuro al Project Meridian.

articles.summary: “Cosa dovranno aspettarsi i soldati ugandesi che saranno mandati nella Striscia?”, si chiede The East African. Kampala ha promesso di inviare 1.200 soldati a Gaza per…
articles.preview: “Cosa dovranno aspettarsi i soldati ugandesi che saranno mandati nella Striscia?”, si chiede The East African. Kampala ha promesso di inviare 1.200 soldati a Gaza per partecipare alla Forza internazionale di stabilizzazione, un dispiegamento militare previsto dal piano di pace di Donald Trump, poi approvato dal Consiglio di sicurezza delle Nazioni Unite. articles.body:
“Cosa dovranno aspettarsi i soldati ugandesi che saranno mandati nella Striscia?”, si chiede The East African. Kampala ha promesso di inviare 1.200 soldati a Gaza per partecipare alla Forza internazionale di stabilizzazione, un dispiegamento militare previsto dal piano di pace di Donald Trump, poi approvato dal Consiglio di sicurezza delle Nazioni Unite. Altri paesi africani che hanno buoni rapporti con gli Stati Uniti e Israele hanno offerto soldati, come il Marocco e la repubblica autoproclamata del Somaliland. “Sperano di entrare nelle grazie di Washington e racimolare qualche beneficio per i propri eserciti”, commenta Le Monde Afrique.

articles.summary: I rischi di una nuova guerra sono molto alti perché rispetto al passato la regione è più instabile, avverte un settimanale etiope
articles.preview: L’Etiopia settentrionale si trova di nuovo sull’orlo di una catastrofe. Gli ultimi scontri tra le forze armate del governo etiope e il Fronte popolare di liberazione del Tigrai indicano che la tregua precaria raggiunta quattro anni fa si sta sgretolando e che i compromessi hanno lasciato il posto a una mentalità a “somma zero”. articles.body:
L’Etiopia settentrionale si trova di nuovo sull’orlo di una catastrofe. Gli ultimi scontri tra le forze armate del governo etiope e il Fronte popolare di liberazione del Tigrai indicano che la tregua precaria raggiunta quattro anni fa si sta sgretolando e che i compromessi hanno lasciato il posto a una mentalità a “somma zero”. Con l’intensificarsi dei movimenti militari, entrambe le parti si sono lanciate in recriminazioni, accusandosi a vicenda di aver sparato il primo colpo. Tuttavia soffermarsi su chi abbia premuto per primo il grilletto è una pericolosa distrazione. Quello che conta ora è la terrificante realtà verso cui porterà questo conflitto se non sarà fermato subito: il completo collasso istituzionale e sofferenze inimmaginabili.

Non ci sono dubbi: la ripresa degli scontri segna la fine dell’accordo di pace firmato a Pretoria, in Sudafrica, nel 2022. Il patto era di far tacere le armi, facilitare il ritorno dell’ordine costituzionale, disarmare i combattenti e garantire l’arrivo di aiuti umanitari. Invece gli impegni politici non sono stati rispettati, si è diffuso un clima di sfiducia e una fragile pace si è disintegrata.

Le ripercussioni si fanno già sentire. La sospensione dei voli commerciali della Ethiopian Airlines verso i principali aeroporti del Tigrai e l’interruzione dei servizi di telecomunicazione mostrano una spirale oscura e fin troppo familiare, perché significa isolare dal mondo esterno una popolazione già vulnerabile, tagliando le linee dei rifornimenti e le arterie commerciali. Se non sarà fermata, questa nuova guerra potrebbe avere conseguenze umanitarie, politiche, economiche e diplomatiche ancora più gravi di quella del 2020–2022. Durante il precedente conflitto si stima che siano morte 600mila persone, con milioni di sfollati e il tessuto della nazione lacerato. In un contesto già reso difficile dall’inflazione, dagli sfollamenti interni e da una siccità persistente potrebbe scoppiare un caos economico. Dal punto di vista politico, un’altra guerra su vasta scala rischia di mandare in pezzi il contratto sociale, creando dei vuoti di potere che nessuna vittoria militare potrà mai colmare.

Influenze esterne

A rendere particolarmente pericolosa la situazione è la rete di intrecci regionali. Rispetto alla guerra precedente, gli allineamenti politici e geopolitici nel Corno d’Africa sono cambiati. La vicina Eritrea, dove i leader nutrono animosità verso Addis Abeba e fanno calcoli strategici riguardo al nord dell’Etiopia, resta una catalizzatrice d’instabilità. Allo stesso tempo la guerra civile in Sudan ha trasformato quello tra i due paesi in un confine poroso, attraversato da un flusso incontrollato di armi e insorti. Che si tratti di stati confinanti o di gruppi armati locali, il coinvolgimento o l’uso di combattenti per procura esterni minaccia di trasformare una disputa interna in una conflagrazione regionale incontrollabile. La risposta della comunità internazionale deve essere rapida, chiara e decisa. La via della guerra è già stata percorsa e porta solo alla rovina. La via del dialogo è indubbiamente piena di difficoltà e compromessi, e richiede ai leader di mettere da parte orgoglio e ambizioni politiche. Le parti in conflitto devono fare un passo indietro dal baratro. Ai libri di storia non interesserà chi ha sparato per primo, ma solo se i leader di questa generazione avranno avuto il coraggio di fermare gli scontri prima che non ci fosse più nulla da salvare. ◆

articles.title: Vannacci è fuorviante sulle cause della guerra in Ucraina

articles.body:
Il 29 settembre il presidente di Futuro Nazionale Roberto Vannacci è stato ospite di Porta a Porta, su Rai1, dove ha commentato i risultati delle elezioni suppletive a Reggio Calabria e le principali questioni del dibattito politico. Tra le altre cose, Vannacci è tornato ad affrontare il tema della guerra in Ucraina, ribadendo la necessità di interrompere il sostegno militare al governo di Volodymir Zelensky.

A sostegno della sua posizione, Vannacci ha ricostruito (-1:29:40) quelle che sarebbero le cause del nuovo conflitto in Ucraina, iniziato dopo l’invasione russa partita il 24 febbraio 2022. «I problemi tra l’Ucraina e la Russia sono cominciati nel 2008 in seguito al vertice della NATO che ha invitato l’Ucraina ad aderire alla NATO», ha detto Vannacci. Secondo il leader di Futuro Nazionale, in quel vertice ci sarebbe stato «l’avvio delle trattative» per l’adesione non solo dell’Ucraina, ma della Georgia e della Moldavia, cosa che non sarebbe stata gradita dal presidente russo Vladimir Putin, che temeva l’allargamento a Est dell’Organizzazione del Trattato dell’Atlantico del Nord (ossia la NATO, ndr). Vannacci ha poi aggiunto che la NATO e l’Ucraina non avrebbero accettato tre «ultimatum» dati da Putin prima dell’invasione. «L’Ucraina non entra nella NATO, non vengono schierate truppe della NATO in Ucraina, non vengono schierati sistemi a lunga gittata della NATO in Ucraina», queste sono le condizioni che Putin avrebbe dato secondo Vannacci e che però non sarebbero state accettate.

Ma le cose stanno davvero così? In breve: Vannacci semplifica troppo le cause del conflitto in Ucraina, creando una narrazione non supportata nel complesso dalle fonti ufficiali. L’affermazione secondo cui i problemi tra Russia e Ucraina sarebbero cominciati nel 2008, in seguito alla decisione della NATO di aprire all’ingresso dell’Ucraina, contiene una parte di verità ma la tesi secondo cui la NATO e l’Ucraina non avrebbero accettato gli “ultimatum” di Putin è fuorviante.

articles.title: Non sono stati sequestrati 140 milioni di dollari negli uffici dell’ex responsabile degli appalti per la difesa ucraina
articles.summary: È una notizia falsa diffusa da un falso sito di un media ucraino e rilanciata dalla propaganda russa
articles.preview: Il 25 settembre 2026 su Facebook è stato pubblicato un presunto servizio del media ucraino The New Voice of Ukraine (NV) in cui una voce di donna fuori campo racconta che l’Ufficio nazionale anticorruzione dell’Ucraina (NABU) avrebbe trovato e «sequestrato oltre 140 milioni di dollari in contanti, stipati in diversi cartoni per frigoriferi» durante un blitz negli uffici di Arsen Zhumadilov, ex capo dell’Agenzia per gli appalti della difesa dimessosi lo scorso 31 agosto in relazione ad accuse di sprechi, frodi e corruzione.
articles.body:
Il 25 settembre 2026 su Facebook è stato pubblicato un presunto servizio del media ucraino The New Voice of Ukraine (NV) in cui una voce di donna fuori campo racconta che l’Ufficio nazionale anticorruzione dell’Ucraina (NABU) avrebbe trovato e «sequestrato oltre 140 milioni di dollari in contanti, stipati in diversi cartoni per frigoriferi» durante un blitz negli uffici di Arsen Zhumadilov, ex capo dell’Agenzia per gli appalti della difesa dimessosi lo scorso 31 agosto in relazione ad accuse di sprechi, frodi e corruzione.

Il servizio continua aggiungendo che su una di queste scatole era stata apposta «un’etichetta con la scritta “Servitore del Popolo”», cioè il nome della serie televisiva satirica scritta e interpretata nel 2015 da Volodymyr Zelensky prima di entrare in politica ed essere eletto nel 2019 presidente dell’Ucraina.

Nel filmato si vedono anche presunti agenti della NABU entrare in una stanza dove si trovano diversi grandi scatoloni con mazzette da 10mila dollari ciascuna. Attaccato all’esterno di uno di essi, si vede un biglietto in ucraino con la scritta «Servitore del Popolo».

È una notizia falsa.

Non esiste alcun riscontro su media credibili e affidabili di un’operazione del NABU negli uffici di Zhumadilov in cui sarebbero stati trovati scatoloni con dentro 140 milioni di dollari. Inoltre, il filmato che mostra gli agenti NABU con gli scatoloni pieni di dollari contiene incongruenze ed errori tipici dei prodotti IA: ad esempio, le mani degli agenti risultano sfocate e non definite in maniera realistica e in ogni mazzetta compare una fascetta con scritte in inglese che contengono in alcuni casi non lettere ma segni incomprensibili.

L’Ufficio nazionale anticorruzione dell’Ucraina ha smentito il 25 settembre 2026 ufficialmente la veridicità di questa notizia infondata, aggiungendo che la scena presente nel video virale che mostra agenti del NABU ritrovare scatoloni pieni di soldi è stata generata con l’intelligenza artificiale. Anche The New Voice of Ukraine ha smentito lo stesso giorno di aver mai pubblicato una simile notizia.

Come hanno ricostruito i fact-checker spagnoli di Maldita e statunitensi di Lead Stories il video in questione attribuito a The New Voice of Ukraine è inizialmente comparso il 23 settembre in un falso sito (ora non più disponibile online, ma qui si può vedere una copia cache) per far credere di essere il media ucraino, creato il 21 settembre (cioè due giorni prima la diffusione della falsa notizia) e avente come dominio «nvukraine.com». Il dominio autentico di The New Voice of Ukraine è invece «nv.ua».

La falsa notizia è stata poi rilanciata il 24 settembre da canali russi su Telegram e ripresa su X in inglese il giorno successivo da una serie di account di propaganda e disinformazione filorussa.

articles.title: OpenAI fires workers for mishandling 'sensitive information'
articles.summary: The former employees were investigated for sharing data with an outside AI evaluation group.
articles.preview: OpenAI has fired three researchers for allegedly mishandling information, including work that involved an external organisation that analyses artificial intelligence (AI) models. "Our investigation confirmed that these individuals mishandled sensitive information outside established company procedures, violating our policies and breaking the trust essential to our work," a spokesperson told the BBC. The ChatGPT-maker did not name the sacked workers, but at least two of them were involved in safety research at the firm.
articles.body:
OpenAI has fired three researchers for allegedly mishandling information, including work that involved an external organisation that analyses artificial intelligence (AI) models.

"Our investigation confirmed that these individuals mishandled sensitive information outside established company procedures, violating our policies and breaking the trust essential to our work," a spokesperson told the BBC.

The ChatGPT-maker did not name the sacked workers, but at least two of them were involved in safety research at the firm.

The firings come as the debate over AI safety and the risks the technology may pose to humanity has intensified in recent weeks.

"We have parted ways with three individuals for violating our policies on accessing and handling sensitive company information," OpenAI's spokesperson said.

The BBC understands the former employees were not let go for raising safety concerns but for allegedly mishandling sensitive information.

Concerns over AI safety have made headlines after some researchers and industry executives called for more guardrails around the technology.

OpenAI has come under under intense scrutiny after its models went rogue and hacked several platforms, including Australian government websites.

In an earlier incident an OpenAI system accessed the internet and breached the open-source developer platform Hugging Face.

That incident led OpenAI to conduct a broad review of the activities of its AI models - called agents, which are designed to execute tasks autonomously based on simple instructions.

The AI lab said this week that it has notified more than 100 organisations about incidents involving unauthoritised activity linked to its AI systems.

Being notified "does not mean that any private information was accessed" or that a system was compromised, OpenAI said.

On Tuesday, US President Donald Trump hosted a meeting of top technology bosses - including leaders from OpenAI, Anthropic, Nvidia, SpaceX, Meta and Google - to discuss AI.

After the gathering at the White House, Trump posted a document that he called a "morally binding" agreement that would serve as a "form of protection" from AI's potential risks.

Some technology experts criticised the pact, pointing out that it allowed AI companies to regulate themselves.

Trump has repeatedly downplayed concerns about AI's risks in response to calls from some industry figures for tighter oversight of the technology.

articles.title: Kevin Mandia’s new ‘agent swarm’ security startup Armadin raises $255.5M at $2.5B valuation

articles.body:
Kevin Mandia, best known as the founder of cybersecurity startup Mandiant, which sold to Google for $5.4 billion in 2022, has raised $255.5 million for his latest startup, Armadin, at a valuation of more than $2.5 billion, the company announced on Thursday.

The Series B round was led by Andreessen Horowitz and Accel, with Bain Capital Ventures, Redpoint, 8VC, Ballistic Ventures, Google Ventures, In-Q-Tel, Kleiner Perkins, and Menlo Ventures joining in.

The new round comes just six months after Armadin raised a $190 million Series A in March. It has now raised more than $445 million.

Armadin is offering enterprises a new kind of always-on security by reimagining defense testing for the AI era. Instead of traditional penetration tests, where hired guns attempt to break in and report on the weaknesses they find, Armadin runs always-on agentic swarms, who chain together vulnerabilities to hack in. The idea is to help organizations find and seal holes before any bad guys (or even AI labs with rogue agents) can use agentic tech against them.
